abstract: Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4–30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent–model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4–21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.

sections.body: The paper observes that each turn of a coding agent bills a persistent prefix plus an growing interaction history, so earlier content is charged repeatedly. Three fixed cost-control strategies (Rust Token Killer, Serena, and Aider's RepoMap) gave mixed effects across repositories. The authors propose TokenEconomizer, an external black-box controller that learns environment-specific policies for micro-skills, tool pruning, and failure-loop intervention from completed traces. On 277 SWE-Bench tasks across 6 repositories, it reduces mean per-task cost by 18.4–30.9% and improves Pass@1 over default execution in 4 of 5 agent–model settings. The authors also evaluate Web-Bench and two security-auditing benchmarks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Recurring coding-agent costs in shared repositories motivate an external controller that learns from completed tasks.

sections.body: The authors profile 60 SWE-Bench tasks, 10 from each of 6 repositories, comparing default execution with Rust Token Killer (RTK), Serena, and RepoMap. No fixed strategy lowered cost consistently: on Django all three reduced cost, while on SymPy all three increased it. In default traces, actions that recur in at least half of a repository's tasks account for 12–28% of the bytes its tool calls send and receive. Of 23 tool schemas loaded on every turn, no repository invokes more than 7, and 16 are never called. Failed executions make up 17% of tasks but 32% of total spend. The authors describe these measurements as upper bounds on achievable savings.
sections.heading: Cost Profiling and Analysis of Fixed Cost-control Strategies
sections.headline: Fixed cost-control strategies give mixed results by repository, and traces reveal three sources of removable cost.

sections.body: TokenEconomizer treats each agent as a black box and acts through the instruction prefix, the loaded tools, and the event stream. Each task receives three decisions. Micro-skills are one-line operational facts, checked by regular-expression and predicate detectors, and a skill is activated only after several confirmations on non-overlapping edited files. Never-called tools are pruned after a fixed unused streak or an LLM judge's irrelevance verdict, and a periodic re-audit restores the full catalog. The turn budget $B_{i}$ is set from a high percentile of prior successful turn counts. A skill retires when its decayed support turns negative, with each contradiction weighted by $\lambda=5$. A stuck verdict redirects the agent first, and a forced stop applies at $\kappa$ times the budget under a strict stall rule.
sections.heading: TokenEconomizer
sections.headline: TokenEconomizer selects micro-skills, tool masks, and turn budgets per repository using confirmation, retirement, and failure-loop rules learned from traces.

sections.body: Five agent–model settings run the same 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, in chronological order within each repository. Comparisons include default execution, default at medium and low effort, RTK, RepoMap, TokenEconomizer, and TokenEconomizer combined with RTK or RepoMap. Table 1 shows that TokenEconomizer alone reduces mean cache-aware cost by 18.4–30.9% in all five settings, with Pass@1 falling only 1.0 percentage point on Opus 4.8. Lower reasoning effort reduces Pass@1 by 1.8–10.3 percentage points. Fig. 5(a) reports 30 repository–setting cells, where TokenEconomizer reduces cost in all 30, by 5.2–40.1%. Results are averages over three seeds.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On the software-engineering benchmark, TokenEconomizer cuts mean cost 18.4–30.9% across five settings, raising Pass@1 in four.

sections.body: The related-work section groups prior work into cost reduction and cross-task experience. Cascades and routers lower cost per query by choosing models, trading quality for cost, whereas TokenEconomizer keeps the model and effort fixed. Existing agent-side methods compress context, narrow retrieval, restrict tools, or add runtime checks, and the authors report that their effects vary across repositories. Prior experience reuse stores verbal lessons, workflows, executable skill libraries, or repository memories. The authors note that indiscriminate repository context can raise cost without improving success, so experience must be reused selectively. TokenEconomizer uses cross-task traces to learn cost-control policies through the interfaces agents already expose.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Existing agent cost methods are typically fixed and task-local, whereas TokenEconomizer adapts cost control from completed traces.

sections.body: The authors list several limits. Each meta-strategy can err: a micro-skill may go stale, a pruned tool may be needed, and a productive task may be mistaken for a failure loop. Stated recovery paths are that a contradicted skill retires, a wrongly pruned tool returns at re-audit, and the guard redirects before it stops. Experiments cover three harnesses but not minimal ones such as Pi, which would need an adapter. SWE-Bench streams consist of related but independent fixes rather than actual user sessions, so continuous sessions are a next test. The conclusion states that an external controller can make an unchanged agent cheaper while largely preserving task success across software engineering, web development, and security auditing.
sections.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
sections.headline: Stale skills, wrongly pruned tools, and mistaken loop detections remain possible, and streams are not real user sessions.

sections.body: Appendix A places TokenEconomizer within a broader class of external controllers and explains the choice of micro-skills as the unit of injected knowledge. Appendix B gives the cost-profiling protocol and the per-repository results in Table 3, and caps RepoMap at a 2,048-token budget. Appendix C gives the shared configuration in Table 4. A micro-skill needs 3 confirmations on non-overlapping edited files and a need rate of at least 0.4 over at least 4 exercises. Unused tools are removed after 3 tasks. The turn budget is 1.25 times the 90th percentile of passed turns, and the forced stop is at 2.5 times the budget. Appendix J describes the harness adapters and the answer-key guard.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers extended discussion, cost-profiling protocol, controller configuration, task selection, examples, and harness customization.
